Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism
I t’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.
The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.
None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.
Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.
A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.
There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system – and that’s where the core problems lie.
Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.
Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies – and, additionally, all other positive intangibles – out of a company in pursuit of those profits.
Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.
From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful … until something bad happens.
But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.
The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyber-attack – both human and AI-fueled – and more susceptible to random mistakes.
The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.
Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.
We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation – with enforcement and meaningful fines – and stringent antitrust enforcement.
But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement – especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.
Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and the University of Toronto’s Munk School

It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers
A I is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.
Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.
The World Economic Forum finds analytical thinking is now the skill employers value most, and estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training to adapt to this shift by 2030.
In September, I found myself at the first Global Brain Economy Summit in New York asking a hard question: How much room is there for creativity and learning when one’s mind is consumed by anxieties about paying rent or for food to last through the week?
There are two new indices that rank countries and US states on brain capital, using about 60 indicators ranging from child poverty to the prevalence of Parkinson’s disease. Yet they both possess a flaw: neither measures whether people’s livelihoods are secure – whether income is predictable, debts are manageable or homes are safe. The World Health Organization counts safety and security among the foundations of brain health, but nobody building these indices asked people what drains their mental capacity.
I call this missing liability “cognitive taxation”. It is a tax no government voted for, levied on attention, memory and the capacity to learn, and collected through rents, debts and welfare paperwork. Worry over insecurity runs in the background like an app draining a phone battery, and over years, the chronic stress wears down the brain itself. And AI is raising the rate.
Livelihood pressures stack up to exceed what one mind can handle. Poverty manufactures its own interest payments. Imagine a week in which a worker’s rent goes up and she loses a shift at the last minute, something common for workers without guaranteed hours. She puts the shortfall on a credit card. Preoccupied with finding the rent, she returns a benefits form late and loses part of her benefits payment as a penalty. Three small setbacks leave her household poorer in money, headspace and health.
Financial scarcity measurably impairs how well people think, but the effect lifts when the pressure does too, according to a 2024 analysis of 112,000 people in the Journal of Economic Psychology. Low-paid workers in rural India who received their wages a few days early were 7% more productive and made fewer mistakes. When South Africa lowered the pension age for men from 65 to 60, those who became eligible earlier showed slower memory decline and were about five percentage points less likely to develop dementia.
Though AI is increasing the value of human judgment, it also increases cognitive taxation. Automation makes work less predictable, shifting and shortening schedules, long before it eliminates jobs, as Walmart staff dealing with AI-set schedules have found. Meanwhile, overseeing AI tools also adds mental fatigue, according to research by the Boston Consulting Group. Workers required to retrain for the AI economy will struggle to learn new skills if their minds are already occupied by worries over pay, housing and debt.
Britain shows what insecurity already costs before AI adds to it. About 2.7 million people there are out of work through long-term sickness. And my institute’s research found that people facing insecurity across several areas of life carry an earnings penalty as large as the gender pay gap, one that roughly doubles after seven years. Those findings suggest that worry erodes how well people work. Now the UK’s AI minister says the government must seriously consider that the tech could have “ an unprecedented impact ” on the jobs market. Worries abound and compound.
When Elon Musk told reporters at the White House in September that AI would bring “universal high income”, he offered Silicon Valley’s favourite answer to job losses: cash. Yet a study funded by Sam Altman, giving low-income Americans $1,000 a month, found that mental health gains faded after the first year. Extra cash helps, but it cannot guarantee a place for your child at a nursery or a bus that gets you to work on time. These pressures already tax the minds of people in work, and no payment removes them.
The better answer to cognitive tax and job loss is universal basic services, providing childcare, housing, transport and digital access, free at the point of use. The principle is the one behind the UK’s National Health Service: people should be able to rely on essential support without facing a bill when they use it. Extending free childcare alone is expected to bring 60,000 non-working parents into jobs in the UK.
Every government should ask this question of every fiscal policy: How will this policy affect the cognitive load of the poorest people it touches? Britain, which takes over the G20 presidency after December’s summit in Miami, should put it to the world’s largest economies. This question belongs in every treasury’s fiscal plans, brain-capital indices and AI-powered public services before they launch.
Sixty years ago we learned to count the damage economies do to the air and water, and it has changed how we build infrastructure for the better. Now that AI is making our minds the most valuable thing we have, it is time we count the damage done to them.
Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

Apple has set the 2026 MacBook lineup. Complete with several MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models, along with the cheaper MacBook Neo, there’s a lot to consider before deciding on the MacBook that best suits your needs.
With a decade of MacBook testing under my belt, I feel confident in my ability to point you in the right direction, regardless of your budgetary restraints and performance needs. Speaking of budget, if you’re hunting for discounts, be aware that Apple recently increased MacBook prices, citing component supply constraints and the high cost of memory and storage chips.
For more recommendations, be sure to check out the rest of our computer buying guides , like the Best Laptops , Best Cheap Laptops , Best iPads , and Best Windows Laptops .
Updated July 2026: I’ve added context behind Apple’s recent price increase for models in its MacBook line.
As of March 2026, Apple has refreshed every MacBook, including the MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, and the new MacBook Neo. That means if you shop now, you’ll get the latest hardware, which may extend its longevity. You’ll also get ongoing software support from Apple.
The problem is that on June 25, Apple dramatically increased the price of all the MacBooks (and iPads) to varying degrees. Here’s a breakdown of the new prices, with increases ranging from $100 to $400:
It’s very rare for Apple to raise prices suddenly, especially when the change doesn’t accompany a product refresh. What makes this update especially unusual, though, is that only a few months have passed since the MacBook Neo launched. Apple blames the price spikes on memory and storage increases, stating that AI data centers have “created an extraordinary surge in demand" never seen before.
So yes, the better time to buy a MacBook would have been earlier this year. While Apple says that it is “working tirelessly to find solutions,” I wouldn’t expect these prices to come down anytime soon. Predictions around how long this memory shortage will last are measured in years, not months.
One potential update to note: A rumored MacBook launch later this year that would be a major moment. It will reportedly sport an OLED display, a touchscreen-optimized interface, an M6 chip, and a thinner chassis. While the device was once believed to be a forthcoming version of the MacBook Pro, a recent report from Bloomberg discusses an alternative high-end machine, possibly known as a MacBook Ultra. If it comes to fruition, it could be a way for Apple to offer a more expensive MacBook that isn’t purely performance-driven.
One other interesting development in the world of Mac rumors is the forthcoming M6 chip, which will reportedly be the first in the lineup that will be a standalone chip that won’t get an M6 Pro, M6 Max, or M6 Ultra. That would render the current M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro the most up-to-date models for longer than usual.
All of Apple’s processors are scattered throughout different MacBook models, and you can find older models at specific third-party retailers online, either completely new or refurbished. If you do stumble upon its older chips (which came out four years ago), you might be wondering how they compare to other options. Here, get a breakdown of the differences to consider.
M5 : The M5 chips are the latest options from Apple, having arrived in late 2025 with the launch of the 14-inch MacBook Pro, iPad Pro, and Vision Pro. The base M5 still has up to a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, though there’s also a lower-tier 9-core CPU that’s available on the iPad Pro . The M5 is around 10 to 15 percent faster in CPU performance but also takes a significant step up in GPU, AI workloads, and even storage speed. Like Apple’s mobile chips, the M5 is now also available on the MacBook Air.
M5 Pro : Currently available exclusively on the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros, the M5 Pro comes with up to an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU. The base configuration starts with only a 15-core CPU and 16-core GPU. As with previous generations, the “Pro” chip gets all the same benefits as those in the M5 architecture but adds more cores and improved memory bandwidth. The biggest advantage is in GPU and on-device AI performance. This time around, however, both the M5 Pro and M5 Max also debuted an update: “Fusion Architecture” is a new version of UltraFusion (which was previously used only on the Ultra chips) that combines two dies together across a superfast interconnect.
M5 Max : The M5 Max is the M5 Pro—only with more GPU power. You get the option for up to 40 GPU cores, which puts the MacBook Pro on the level of high-end gaming laptops in terms of graphics performance. Add in the neural accelerators that are now built into each GPU core, and you’ve got one of the most powerful AI laptops on the market. In terms of Apple rankings, it’s only bested in GPU performance by the M3 Ultra, which is currently available only in the Mac Studio.
M4: The M4 originally launched in 2024. It has a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU. Apple claims the M4 delivers 1.8 times faster CPU performance and 2.2 times faster GPU performance than the M1. Meanwhile, the neural engine is more than three times faster than the original and twice as fast as the M3. It also starts with 16 GB of unified memory, which helps to power Apple Intelligence (the company’s suite of artificial intelligence features) more smoothly. It’s available on the 14-inch MacBook Pro (2024) , iMac (2024) , and MacBook Air ( 13-inch and 15-inch , 2025).
M4 Pro: The M4 Pro has a 14-core CPU (which Apple claims is up to 1.9 times faster than the M1 Pro) and up to a 20-core GPU, with up to 64 GB of unified memory. Built on a second-generation 3-nanometer process, it also supports enhanced GPU features like mesh shading and ray tracing—the latter of which is now twice as fast as on M3 chips. You’ll find it on the 2024 MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) and Mac Mini (2024) .
M4 Max: This chip has a 16-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU with support for up to 128 GB of unified memory. Apple says the CPU is up to 2.2 times faster than the M1 Max, while the GPU is up to 1.9 times faster. As with the M4 Pro, it packs support for mesh shading and ray tracing. The M4 Max is available as an option on the 2024 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro , and you can also get it as an option in the current Mac Studio.
M3: The M3 was available on the 14-inch MacBook Pro (late 2023), 13-inch MacBook Air (2024), 15-inch MacBook Air (2024), and 24-inch iMac (2023). It packs an 8-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU with 24 GB of unified memory. When compared with the M1, Apple claimed CPU performance was up to 35 percent faster, and GPU performance was up to 65 percent faster. The company said the CPU and GPU are both 20 percent faster than the M2. As with the M1 and M2, it was great for basic tasks like word processing, sending emails, using spreadsheets, and light gaming. With the 13-inch and 15-inch MacBook Air, you also had support for two external displays (one display with up to 6K resolution at 60 Hz and another with up to 5K resolution at 60 Hz).
M3 Pro: With a 12-core CPU and an 18-core GPU, Apple claimed the M3 Pro's GPU was only up to 10 percent faster than the M2 Pro, making it a marginal upgrade from its predecessor. Compared with the M1 Pro, however, the M2 Pro was up to 40 percent faster in GPU performance and 20 percent faster in CPU performance. It was available on the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2023. It was the ideal in-between for those who needed a chip that was more powerful than the M3 but wouldn't use the full power of the M3 Max.
M3 Max: This was the next step up from the M2 Max. It had a 16-core CPU, 40-core GPU, and up to 128 GB of unified memory. According to Apple, the CPU performance was up to 80 percent faster than the M1 Max and up to 50 percent faster than the M2 Max. REI's 2026 Holiday Sale kicked off November 13 and lasts until November 23. There are plenty of great deals to help you restock your backpacking, hiking, biking, camping, outdoor loving gear quiver. REI members can use the code HOLIDAY2026 to save an extra 20 percent off one full-price item and an extra 20 percent off one REI Outlet item. Below are the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more.
There are also sales at Backcountry.com and some of our favorite cottage industry brands like Six Moon Designs , Zenbivy , and more. Not sure what you need? Check out our many outdoor gear guides .
The 650 Down Jacket is one of the best budget three-season puffer jackets you can buy, more so at this price. At 10.9 ounces, it's reasonably lightweight and has large hand pockets and some very nice internal pockets for stashing a hat or gloves. The kids' version is also on sale in a nice yellow color that's handy for spotting your child in the snow.
The Ghost Whisperer Down Jacket is my top pick for a backpacking puffer jacket . It weighs just 6.7 ounces for a men's medium (7.3 ounces for the men's large I tested), packs down to a tiny little thing (stuffing into its own pocket), and the 1,000-fill-power goose down offers one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios on the market. The men's version is technically on sale right now , but the only size available is small and XXL.
This is my favorite puffer jacket, especially in the shoulder seasons when temps dip a little lower. It features 4.5 ounces of 1,000-fill down (men’s medium), which is half the weight of the overall jacket. The internal TILT lining (short for Thermo Ionic Lining Technology) may or may not do anything; I haven't been able to devise an effective test, but even if it did nothing, the amount of 1,000-fill-power down combined with the scant weight makes this an appealing option for ultralighters. The 7D fabric (which is what keeps the weight low) does need babying, but I haven't had any issues in over a year of use.
This is great deal on a very warm down parka. It's thigh-length, which helps keep drafts up your back to a minimum, and it fits pretty well, though it's definitely boxy (what do you want from a 650-down-fill parka that's designed primarily to keep you warm?). I did find that the main two-way zipper can be fiddly, and does sometimes snag, but it's hardly a deal-breaker, especially at this price.
This 850-fill down hoodie makes the honorable mentions section of our puffer jacket guide. The cut is roomy and its gusseted around the shoulders for climbing. Our main gripe is that it's pricey, but this deal takes some of sting out of the price. The women's version is unfortunately not on sale.
The Rainier is our favorite budget rain jacket , especially when it's on sale. Unlike most rain jackets in this price range, the Rainier uses high-quality three-layer, seam-taped, laminate waterproofing that's non-fluorinated (meaning no PFAS). It has some other features rare in budget rain jackets, like pit zips or venting, a weatherproof center zip, and an adjustable, stowable hood.
It's a little weird to shop for sun hoodies with snow on the way, but if you're looking to avoid the sun next summer, REI's Sahara Shade hoodie is a great alternative to sunscreen. I don't often use a sun hoodie myself, but I have worn this one and it does do a good job of protecting you without feeling too stuffy on a hot day (it's definitely better for protecting against high altitude sun rather than humid, Florida sun).
When these were an REI Outlet deal earlier this year I got nervous that they might be discontinued, but apparently not because they are back. REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides when I'm riding my bike, but if you prefer, the regular top is also on sale for $64 , as is the base layer bottom .
Smartwool's 100 percent merino base layer is my top pick for cooler weather in our guide to the best base layers . It's a great all-around choice, and the loose fit makes it work as a long-sleeve T-shirt in the shoulder seasons. That extra bit of roominess makes it possible to use it as a second light layer over something thinner. The pants are also on sale for $94 ($31 off) .
Keen's Targhee Apex has finally found a look that isn't bad by Targhee standards. Perhaps more than any other shoe we've tested, these look like the trail-running Gorpcore icons they are. At just 0.75 pounds each, they are light without being fragile, and the generous footbed lets your feet spread comfortably on long days.
The La Sportiva Prodigio combines trail-running agility with boot-level protection, delivering surprising versatility on rugged terrain. They're one of our favorite light hiking boots . The fit is a little on the snug side—much like La Sportiva climbing shoes—but they should be fine even for wide feet thanks to the generous footbed width. At 1.65 pounds for the pair, these aren't terribly bulky, either.
These are my favorite barefoot sandals . I always refer to these as the barefoot equivalent of Chaco sandals. They're not as robust—I'd still bring Chacos for white-water rafting—but for everything else, these are perfect. Z-Trails flex and bend as you walk, giving your feet the freedom of movement you'd expect from a barefoot shoe, though these do have 10 mm of cushioning, which makes them a good option if you're just starting out with barefoot shoes. The even more minimal Z-Trek sandals are also on sale for $45 ($15 off) .
These Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers are my favorite hiking pants thanks the thigh zips that deliver excellent ventilation. The Vidda Pros uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere, and nice reinforced knees (with openings for pads). There's even a hatchet loop on the leg.
Six Moon Design's Lunar Solo is one of the best single-wall ultralight solo tents you can buy. It's not without its quirks ( read the pitching tips ), but if you want something more than a tarp, that still weighs just 26 ounces (740 grams), this one is hard to beat. Use the Code YULEHIKE to get the 25 percent off.
Nemo's Hornet tents are some of the lightest freestanding tents around. The 1-person model is my go-to for situations where I might have to pitch on rock or concrete slabs (like staying in towns on a longer bike-packing trip). It's roomy enough for you and all your gear, light enough at 2.25 pounds (without stakes), and packs down remarkably small. It's also held up well in storms, though you will want some extra guy-outs if the wind is really howling (I like Zpacks 1.2-mm dyneema cord for lightweight guy lines).
This is the bike-packing version of Big Agnes' popular Copper Spur tent, one of the best backpacking tents around. The only difference, aside from color, is that the pole segments on this model are shorter (to make it easier to store on a bike). The Copper Spur line is very nearly the lightest freestanding tent around (it's just slightly heavier than the Hornet above), and if you happen to use it with trekking poles, you get what I think is the best feature, the covered awning modification for the vestibule. While this is the best deal, the 2-person model is also on sale for 20 percent off .
This is one of my favorite ultralight sleeping bags . There are lighter quilts out there, but when you need the warmth of a mummy bag on those colder nights, this is what I use. It also has the smallest pack size of any bag I've tested in this temperature range. With the included compression sack, this thing is truly tiny. The down fill is PFC-free, 850+ hydrophobic down. The zippers are on the small side, but they slide well and rarely (if ever) snag on the bag. I've slept in this bag down to 20 degrees and never been the least bit cold.

Stressed? Heart rate elevated? If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura , Ultrahuman , or Samsung , the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing exercises, meditations, or a physical reset like a short walk. So far, so Silicon Valley. But now you can add reading the Bible to that list of self-soothing activities.
The first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps . Two new devices in particular—Glorify’s Ring and Everblessed Technology’s Elah Ring—connect to hugely popular Christian prayer apps with tens of millions of users, and both claim to be the world’s first Christian smart ring.
Both are first, in their own ways. Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US. The $299 Glorify Ring launched in July, with reservations open and shipping set for January 2027, but 77,000 units of an earlier beta iteration, the Amen Ring made by faith tech company ConfideIn (which merged with Glorify this May), were given away last Christmas. Everblessed manages the Blessed app, and Glorify has an eponymous app.
Another big player in prayer apps is Hallow , aimed at Catholics, backed by Vice President JD Vance’s Narya venture capital firm and celebrity ambassadors, with 24 million installs to date. Hallow’s toe-dip into wearables was a 2024 smart rosary with NFC embedded in the crucifix, made with Italian brand Ghirelli; Everblessed tried an earbud, necklace, and bedside device before settling on the ring design.
Head-to-head on design, the Elah and Glorify rings are both made from titanium alloy, with a thorn-inspired twist for Glorify and a minimalist band featuring a cross for the Elah S1, which is also IP68 waterproof to 5 meters.
For now, the Elah Ring is slightly techier: prayer reminders come via the cross, which glows via an LED, and “gentle” vibrations; these can pulse at certain times of day or be triggered by changes in heart rate and stress levels, picked up by a photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor. Glorify’s CEO Henry Costa tells WIRED these emotion-based reminders will land on the Glorify Ring in six months; for now, you can set the times of day you want prayer reminders, track heart rate, blood oxygen, stress, and sleep via the optical sensor.
One addition to the Glorify Ring that Costa says he personally uses “a lot” is recording prayers straight into the built-in mic. The ring has a light to signal when it's recording, and the app transcribes them. Everblessed CEO Ricky Xia says that, after consulting with pastors and users, the feeling was that voice notes on the ring were seen as “suspicious.” It’s available in-app, but most people don’t pray out loud, and too many features drain the battery life. (The Elah Ring runs for up to six days on one charge; Glorify for four to five days.)
Both companies see the smart ring nudges helping wearers prioritize meaningful quiet time, away from screens, while offering in-app Christian practices as an alternative to Eastern meditation. Glorify offers Bible study, courses, and meditations. Blessed has devotional “anchors,” Bible texts and audio, plus guided breathing. Xia says he’s happy if the Elah vibrates and a user picks up a paper Bible rather than the Blessed app, while Costa says he’s “crying out to use my phone less.”
Both Glorify (founded in 2020, now merged with ConfideIn and headquartered in the San Francisco Bay Area) and Blessed (founded in 2023 and based in San Jose) operate in more than 150 countries. Perhaps the biggest difference between the two rings is their relationship to AI.
Xia is all-in, describing the S1 as an “AI-native” product, with a pastor-complementing, not-replacing FaithMate chatbot in the Blessed app, customized based on preferences, congregation, and depth of learning. ChatGPT is like a “good coworker,” he says, while FaithMate is designed to be “your friend” and an agent that can also handle secular tasks.
“A lot of our users not only ask questions about the Bible but also ask about themselves, their relationships with their wives, they’re being bullied at school," Xia says, stressing safeguards around data storage, encryption, and privacy. "Everyone is going to have some AI that they trust, and how they view that is built on their personal stuff, their private vulnerabilities.”
Costa is more circumspect, treading carefully on the consumer-facing side and noting that the Pope has weighed in with a 6,000-word encyclical on AI. A launch interview with CBN News garnered negative comments: “AI is Antichrist Information,” for one.
“The stance I’ve always taken is that our daily devotional is hand-authored by a team of theologians,” Costa says. “It’s prayed over, and that is a stamp of approval.” He criticizes AI slop prayer apps as inauthentic. Still, he says the Glorify team has already tested “many forms” of AI personalization: “Any time, if we do use AI, it must be very clear to the user.”
Smart ring owners were finding ways to add faith features to mainstream accessories before these rings came to fruition. For 20 years, timer and reminder apps have helped with prayer schedules, but recent examples are more creative. Heidi Campbell, professor of communication in religious studies at Texas A&M , refers to these DIY upgrades to the Oura ring and devices like the Muse headband as “spiritual mind-body hacking.”
Oura owners on #christiantiktok chat about how they already use the ring’s stress and HR alerts as a prompt to pause and reflect, as per Elah.
Smart ring users flag changes in resting heart rate and sleep quality with scripture following their daily practice. “It’s really helpful for, like, what was inhibiting me from getting to a meditative or contemplative prayer state?” Campbell says. “It takes some of the mystery out of prayer, I think, but that can also be positive. There is a way to do prayer well and not well.” Ring hackers can also dig into health stats during Lent, Ramadan, and Yom Kippur to analyze energy expenditure and how fasting periods affect their bodies.
The connected Christian ring is likely to remain niche, but that doesn’t mean the products will flop. James Stables, head of communications at smart ring manufacturer Ultrahuman , notes that attaching Christian practices to a trending category feels like a smart play. “Like prayer beads, the ring is analog in its on-body form and kind of tactile and haptic," he says.
AI-powered voice recordings and emerging attempts at emotion tracking are part of a new phase for smart rings, says Ekta Mittal, a senior analyst of connected devices at CCS Insight . These new “purpose-driven” features extend wearable tech into “new parts of consumers’ daily routines,” Mittal says. She suggests that while Glorify and Everblessed will add value for some, the rings are “not directly competing” with established smart ring giants like Oura , Ultrahuman, and Samsung.
The pandemic sped up the digital transition of many places of worship when congregations could not meet up in person, encouraging experimentation with social media. So it’s early days for Silicon Valley’s impact on organized religion. Researchers at the University of Würzburg in Germany, led by Ilona Nord , are studying the theological implications of using tech, including smart rings, for spiritual practices, investigating which values are baked into secular devices and apps.
Campbell suggests many Christian groups haven’t stopped to consider the unintentional consequences of cultivating spirituality via personal tech. “All of these things are about individualizing the practice, which is good, but the challenges are for religions which are really focused on communal aspects,” she says. Not everyone has the money or connectivity to access these gadgets, but also, more existentially, “it puts spiritual development over communal development.”

For refugees, the ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide is a vindication. But for many, the relief comes with a question: will they be able to return home?
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile phone from her shelter in Camp 1E of the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She had been waiting for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) verdict since the afternoon. But poor internet connectivity kept interrupting the live broadcast.
Then she opened Facebook and saw a headline: “ICJ confirms Myanmar committed genocide.”
Overwhelmed, she jumped. Her sister-in-law was cooking. Ruman rushed to hug her. Before she could explain what had happened, she broke down in tears.
“I celebrated with tears of joy because, for the first time, the world acknowledged what happened to us,” she said.
On Thursday, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during brutal military operations in 2017, in which the court found more than 10,000 people had been killed.
The landmark judgement in the case, brought before the court by The Gambia, recognised the atrocities committed against the community after years of denial. For refugees who have spent nearly a decade waiting for justice, the ruling brought a wave of relief, emotion and renewed hope.
“For me, this is not simply a legal verdict. It is proof of our suffering,” Ruman said.
Across the camps, people followed the announcement on mobile phones, laptops and large screens. Some watched with friends. Others gathered with their families. Many turned to Facebook and YouTube to follow the proceedings.
Eighteen-year-old Mohammad Rehan watched with his community teacher and friends on a laptop. “Some women were crying, while others were praying to Allah,” he said. “I did not do anything special. I just sat there and listened, hoping to hear some good news that would give us a peaceful life in the future.”
For Rehan, the first thought was that the verdict could potentially open the door for the Rohingya to return home. “Just imagining that made me so happy,” he said.
The news soon spread through the blocks. Rehan said people were celebrating, while elderly refugees discussed the case and The Gambia’s role in bringing it before the court. The small West African nation was not directly affected by the violence against the Rohingya. Still, it acted as a party to the 1948 Genocide Convention, under which all member states have an obligation to prevent and address genocide. In 2022, the court ruled that The Gambia had standing to bring the case.
Rehan’s mother was also delighted when he told her about the ruling. “She was saying that we had won and that we would be able to return to our homeland,” he said.
The celebrations came against a backdrop of difficult living conditions. Rain fell over the camps on Thursday as Cyclone Akvan bore down on the Bay of Bengal, adding to the discomfort of families living in cramped shelters.
It was a reminder that while the verdict had brought recognition to their suffering, it had not changed the daily realities of refugee life. Nurul Amin, a Rohingya youth, said he was happy when the court recognised the genocide, but the announcement also brought back painful memories.
“I was happy, but I was also remembering what happened to us in 2017. I was remembering the horrific military operation, the violence I experienced and the home I had to leave behind,” he said.
Rohingya activist Rohimullah said the announcement was difficult to put into words. It reminded him of those the community had lost and the darkest days of their displacement. He described the judgement as a moment of relief and renewed hope, but said it could not bring back loved ones or erase painful memories.
Nasir Uddin, a professor of anthropology at the University of Chittagong who researches the Rohingya crisis, said the ICJ ruling was important to ensure justice and accountability from the victims’ perspective.
“In the 21st century, we talk about liberal democracy, globalisation and global justice. Yet such a massive genocide happened before our eyes. The judgement was essential to establish the concept of global justice,” he said.
Michael Kugelman, a resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, said the ruling meant that Dhaka would need stronger assurances from Myanmar about the safe return of Rohingya refugees under any repatriation arrangement.
“I think that this will also have some impact on the dynamics around negotiations between Bangladesh and Myanmar on the return of Rohingya refugees, now that an international court has said that they experienced genocide,” Kugelman told Al Jazeera.
For the Rohingya, however, the hope of going home remains central. They want accountability for those responsible for the atrocities, the restoration of their rights and citizenship, and a safe and dignified return to Myanmar.
Nurul Amin said he hoped the international community would look beyond the humanitarian crisis and address the political causes of their displacement. He said he wanted freedom in Myanmar, democracy and an end to discrimination and military dictatorship.
“We are hoping this judgement will lead to something more – that we will finally be able to return home with our rights and dignity,” he said.

For the protesters in San Francisco, the issue went far beyond financial metrics: their demands centred on strict government regulation, public accountability and guaranteeing that human beings never relinquish control over increasingly powerful machines.

TP-Link’s struggle illustrates how Trump admin wields control over device makers.
TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn’t been able to obtain an exemption.
The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.
While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.
TP-Link’s struggle is not much of a surprise, given its history as a Chinese company and the Trump administration’s focus on reducing reliance on Chinese and other foreign technology. While TP-Link faces political challenges related to the Trump administration’s push for on-shoring, its problems go deeper: It must convince the government its routers aren’t vulnerable to foreign hacking campaigns and that its routers are not Chinese-controlled technology, as suggested at a Congressional committee hearing last year.
TP-Link was founded in 1996 in China but has since split into two companies, with one in the US. The US-based TP-Link established California as global headquarters in October 2024, months after completing a “formal organizational separation” from the TP-Link entity in China.
“TP-Link has split from and no longer has any affiliation with TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd., which serves the mainland Chinese market. Despite having similar names, these companies have entirely different ownership, management, and operations,” TP-Link says .
TP-Link opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Archer 8 Ultra, in September, though not in the US. It’s expected to ship this month and costs £899.99 in the UK, or about $1,178. Since it’s priced like a luxury device, its unavailability in the US won’t make a difference to most consumers. But it’s unknown how long it will take TP-Link to gain permission to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, or whether it will receive permission at all.
TP-Link has pledged to assemble all new routers in the US, but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task. The government reviews of router makers’ requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy. From the outside, it is unclear whether the Trump administration applies consistent security criteria to all companies or whether it grants waivers to favored companies without regard to the actual security of their products.
Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews. SpaceX’s Starlink division obtained a waiver for its routers, while Amazon received a waiver covering routers for its Leo satellite broadband service and the devices sold by its Eero subsidiary. There have been 26 waivers issued so far, covering products made by firms such as Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax, and Vantiva.
Some US lawmakers seem to think the FCC process covers too many products. House Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) and Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) proposed legislation in September that would limit the FCC’s authority to place entire categories of equipment on the list of banned products, as it did with routers.
The Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require the FCC to report to Congress a week before adding any new technology or service to what’s known as the Covered List and require new additions to include only technologies or services produced or provided by an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. That means China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran.
“The current process for identifying and barring malicious foreign technology has worked in many cases, but lacks the transparency, consistency, and clarity needed to meet our long-term national security needs as technology rapidly advances,” Pallone and Guthrie said in a joint statement.
The Pentagon declined Ars’ request for comment on TP-Link’s request for an exemption. The FCC and Department of Homeland Security did not provide any comment.
The US ban on all foreign routers was part of a dramatic expansion of the Covered List, which is managed by the FCC in consultation with the Commerce Department and federal agencies with national security expertise. The Covered List was created by a 2020 law and received its first additions in March 2021. It applies to products that “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”
For the first few years of the Covered List’s existence, only specific companies were added. This included Chinese device-makers Huawei and ZTE, several video surveillance product makers, the Russian security company Kaspersky Lab, and several Chinese telecom companies. Under the Trump administration, new additions to the list include entire product categories, regardless of whether a particular vendor has been identified as a risk. In addition to routers, the Covered List currently includes foreign drones, robotic devices, and power inverters.
A former government official told Ars that the Covered List isn’t as useful as it should be.
“The government needs to be able to quickly identify national security risks and, to the extent that they can, you’ve got to give the public and industry guidance on what to do in order to avoid that risk,” said Betsy McIntyre, a lawyer and consultant who previously worked for the FCC on telecom mergers and at the Department of Justice on national security reviews of foreign investment in telecom. “That’s why I have always loved the Covered List. It’s this great tool. It’s simple. It has so much potential to guide procurement decisions for small businesses, large businesses. It can even help when moms are going to Best Buy and figuring out what kinds of equipment they should be buying.”
McIntyre doesn’t like the approach of adding entire categories of products to the list, rather than specific products from individual companies.
“The ideal Covered List would be, as soon as there’s a problem, it would be updated,” she said. “They’d name a company, and then people know: ‘don’t buy this’ or ‘this kind of equipment poses a national security risk.’ It’s a little bit muddled now.”
Although the FCC maintains the Covered List, McIntyre said the FCC’s role was set up at the beginning to be “very ministerial.” The FCC would add companies or products to the list based on determinations by national security agencies, with the FCC having no discretion once it received a determination.
McIntyre noted that she was not privy to any of the discussions that led to the broad inclusion of routers this year. It’s not necessarily clear to the public why any particular item is added to the list or why any company receives an exemption because “the national security decision-making process can be a black box,” she said.
TP-Link routers formed the bulk of a botnet controlled by Chinese threat actors, Microsoft said in 2024. But TP-Link is far from the only router maker whose products have vulnerabilities. Routers made by US companies Cisco and Netgear were part of a botnet of devices hijacked by Chinese state-sponsored attackers in 2023, the Justice Department said after taking action to remove the malware .

Apple, kullanıcıların bilgisayarlarında çeşitli görevleri yerine getirebilen yeni bir yapay zeka ajanı üzerinde çalışıyor. Şirketin yayımladığı iş ilanları , geliştirilen sistemin internette gezinebildiğini, uygulamalar arasında işlem yapabildiğini ve yazılım kodu yazabildiğini gösteriyor.
Apple'ın bu hamlesi, OpenAI, Anthropic ve Meta gibi şirketlerle rekabetini yeni bir boyuta taşıyabilir. Apple, bilgisayarları kullanıcı adına yönetebilen bir yapay zeka asistanının geliştirilmesini yönetecek üst düzey bir mühendislik yöneticisi arıyor. Şu anda yayından kaldırılmış olan iş ilanında, bir insan gibi bilgisayar kullanabilen, farklı uygulamalarda çalışabilen ve karmaşık görevleri tamamlamak için uygun araçları seçebilen bir yapay zeka sistemi tarif ediliyordu.
İş ilanındaki açıklamaya göre yapay zeka ajanının internet tarayıcıları, uygulamalar, komut satırları ve farklı yazılım hizmetleri arasında geçiş yapması hedefleniyor. Sistem, birden fazla aşamadan oluşan görevleri planlayabilecek ve gerektiğinde farklı alanlarda uzmanlaşmış diğer yapay zeka ajanlarından yararlanabilecek. Apple, bu işlemlerin kullanıcı gizliliğini koruyacak şekilde gerçekleştirilmesini de öncelikleri arasında gösteriyor. Ancak söz konusu özelliklerin şu an için şirketin geliştirme hedefleri olarak konumlandığını ve bu anlamda kullanıma hazır bir üründen bahsedilmediğini belirtelim.
Apple'ın kendi yapay zeka ajanı üzerinde çalışırken üçüncü taraf uygulamaların Mac bilgisayarları kontrol etmesine yönelik güvenlik önlemlerini artırması da dikkat çekiyor.
Şirket, 16 Kasım'da yayımladığı resmi açıklamada macOS 27.3'ün ikinci beta sürümüyle uygulamaların bilgisayardaki verilere erişimini daha ayrıntılı biçimde yönetmeye olanak tanıyan değişiklikler duyurdu.
Yeni düzenlemeler kapsamında kullanıcılar, uygulamalara yalnızca ihtiyaç duydukları dosya ve klasörler için erişim izni verebilecek. Ayrıca yapay zeka ajanlarının her işlem öncesinde yeniden izin istemesi sağlanabilecek. Bir uygulama başka bir uygulamayı kontrol ettiğinde ise kullanıcıya bu durumu bildiren bir uyarı gösterilecek.
Bloomberg'ün haberine göre yeni izin süreçleri, rakip yapay zeka ajanlarının Mac üzerinde çalışmasını daha zahmetli hale getiriyor. Örneğin ChatGPT'nin bilgisayar kontrolü özelliklerini etkinleştirmek için gereken işlem sayısının dört adımdan 14 adıma çıktığı belirtiliyor.
Bununla birlikte Apple, düzenlemelerin amacının kullanıcıların kişisel verilerini korumak olduğunu savunuyor. Şirketin resmi açıklamasında, üçüncü taraf yapay zeka ajanlarının engelleneceğine yönelik bir ifade bulunmuyor.

The ICJ has ruled against Myanmar, but safe return, citizenship and reparations remain far from guaranteed.
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice did something it had never done in its 80-year history: It held a state responsible for committing genocide . By nine votes to six, the court found that Myanmar’s 2017 campaign against the Rohingya crossed the gravest threshold in international law.
That matters because Myanmar’s defence was never simply that nothing terrible happened. It argued that its “clearance operations” followed attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) and were, however brutal, fundamentally counterterrorism. Genocide requires more than proof of killing, rape or village destruction; it requires specific intent to destroy a protected group.
The court found that Myanmar’s government forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence, inflicted extreme violence on children and attacked people fleeing towards Bangladesh. Taking the evidence together, it concluded that the “only reasonable inference” was an intention to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.
That strips away the central evasion of the past decade. The ARSA attacks were real. So was armed conflict. But rebellion is not a legal alibi for genocide. Nor can the atrocities now be dismissed as excesses by rogue soldiers. This was a judgement about what Myanmar, as a state, did to a people.
The 9-6 split will inevitably be used by Myanmar to cast doubt on the ruling. But the judgement is final and binding. And by 10 votes to five, the court went further, ordering reparations, including safe, voluntary and dignified return, family reunification, restitution of property and compensation where restitution is impossible.
For Rohingya survivors, that is extraordinary vindication. Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the courtroom, called it “a great day for the Rohingya”. In Cox’s Bazar, refugees had been making an equally practical demand: They want to go home, but with rights, citizenship and dignity .
But here is the problem: You cannot eat a judgement. You cannot live inside one. You cannot rebuild a burned village with one or raise a child safely inside one.
The ICJ has no enforcement arm. Under Article 94(2) of the United Nations Charter, noncompliance can be taken to the UN Security Council (UNSC), where China or Russia could block action. That makes pressure outside the UNSC essential: Targeted sanctions, ASEAN diplomacy, the ICC investigation and Argentina’s universal-jurisdiction case, where arrest warrants have already been issued for 25 suspects.
Who governs the map has also changed. In 2017, Myanmar’s military dominated Rakhine. Today, the Arakan Army controls most of it, and UN investigators have documented forced recruitment, movement restrictions, arbitrary killings and other abuses against Rohingya under its rule.
Any serious return framework must therefore deal with whoever controls the ground. Bangladesh should tie cross-border trade, humanitarian access and political engagement with the Arakan Army to measurable Rohingya benchmarks: Freedom of movement, restoration of land, an end to forced recruitment, international monitoring and a pathway to citizenship. Dhaka should also press Myanmar’s authorities, ASEAN, China, India, Gulf states and Western governments to support a monitored return-and-reparations mechanism. For too long, ports, pipelines and trade corridors have been treated as “strategic” while the Rohingya remain in the humanitarian file.
Everyone wants something from Myanmar. The Rohingya should finally be part of the bill.
None of this matters if the camps fall apart before return becomes possible. About 95 percent of Rohingya refugees are moderately to highly vulnerable and rely almost entirely on humanitarian assistance. The UN’s scaled-down 2026 response plan seeks $710.5m, 26 percent less than the previous year’s appeal. In April, the World Food Programme reduced support for about two-thirds of refugees under a new tiered system; about 17 percent now receive only $7 per person per month.
Donors applauding the verdict should fund the wait as seriously as they praise the destination. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, which backed The Gambia’s case, and Gulf donors have a particular responsibility. Western governments should restore cuts, while lenders and donors should support Bangladeshi host communities. Underfunded camps feed trafficking, exploitation and dangerous sea journeys towards Malaysia and Indonesia. A judgement that opens a path home is worth little if the people it was meant for cannot survive the wait.
Reparations now have legal force, not merely moral appeal. Property claims should be documented; land restored where possible; compensation paid where it cannot. Aid says: You are suffering, so we will help you survive. Reparations say: A wrong was done to you, and someone is obliged to repair it.
The verdict is enormous. The test now is simpler: Can the Rohingya go home as citizens, reclaim their land, receive compensation and raise their children somewhere other than a refugee camp?
The court has established the truth. Now justice has to bring it home.

Two sides find provisional compromise on scheme but food and farming negotiations go down to the wire
British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that its students should pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a concession to get the deal over the line.
The UK had strongly resisted EU text on the table committing it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but a compromise was hammered out before 10pm, with a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.
Brussels insiders said the EU had kicked the can down the road and agreed not to mention the tuition fees rate in the declaration, with further negotiations to follow in the next six months.
As talks went into the night, EU sources suggested both sides were on track for an agreement within the next day.
On Friday morning, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham , said the UK and Europe were “stronger together”, adding: “The test for this summit is simple: does it make life better for people in Britain? That is what I will deliver in Brussels today – cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the BBC that Burnham’s approach amounted to a “betrayal”. He said: “He’s trying to do it incrementally but it’s perfectly clear that this very very soon becomes a debate about do we rejoin or do we stay out.”
But he acknowledged that for food exporters a deal on agricultural standards would make things “a little bit easier”.
On the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said.
There also seemed to be a compromise by France after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.
The UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards that France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start. Instead, the UK will be consulted on new food laws, but the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.
Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.
It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year .
With less than 24 hours to go before Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some sticking points.
Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”
A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP , including the highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.
Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”
According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules. An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK. “Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.
The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.
The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.
The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state. The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.
Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit
Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.
The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.
The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.
A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.
Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.
The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.
"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun , external , said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.
He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.
Appearing on BBC Breakfast on Friday, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage described the agreement as a "very, very expensive and costly error" and said Burnham has no "democratic mandate to do any of this".
He added that the Labour party manifesto was clear that the UK would not go back towards the single market and asked: "Where is our democracy?".
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".
"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal on food and drink, emissions trading and a new youth mobility scheme, Downing Street has said, although talks on the level of tuition fees EU students will pay remains unresolved.
“ The deal is done – negotiations have concluded, ” a No 10 spokesperson said, less than an hour after Andy Burnham arrived at the summit venue in Brussels, where he was greeted by Ursula von der Leyen , the European Commission president, António Costa , the European Council president.
“Now, both sides will work towards implementation of the youth mobility scheme, the SPS deal and the emissions trading scheme. Both sides have agreed when these will come into force. And those dates are set out in the joint statement, which will be published in due course.
As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place. And talks will continue on some areas – these will be set out in the joint statement later.”
EU sources are damping down fears that there will be no deal until the tuition fees agreement is made.
The bottom line, said one diplomat, is that “the UK has agreed to cut fees”.
Everyone has known for some time they said that the implementation of both the SPS deal (1 March 2028) and youth mobility (between 2028 and 2030) would take more than a year.
Everyone expects the overall reset deal to be done and a compromise to be eventually reached on tuition fees.
But the EU has form with the UK on linking bad behaviour with penalties so the EU statement that the SPS deal and the electricity deal will not be “adopted” until the tuition agreement is achieved needs to be seen as a real threat.
Back in 2020 the EU and the UK agreed that Britain could have associate membership of Horizon Europe . It was a hard fought deal with the UK almost pulling out over a row on the level of rebate owing to London if it did not receive research grants to the value of the UK’s contribution.
The EU, much to the amazement of the UK and the science community, withheld that associate membership until late 2023 in a broader row over the UK’s failure to implement the Northern Ireland protocol in full.
After the deal was announced, UK officials pushed back strongly against the idea that the three plans could be jeopardised if there was no agreement on tuition fees, saying they were completely separate.
Earlier, EU officials had indicated that progress on the main deals would be contingent on tuition fees.
But while talks on tuition fees are scheduled to last another six months, even if there was not agreement by March 2028, when the new arrangements on food and agriculture come into force, this would still happen, UK officials insisted.
They said the UK had also won agreement in principle for sign-up to the EU’s still-to-be finalised “Made in Europe” policy, a protectionist plan intended to limit China’s increasing influence on European industry, with one official calling this “a big win”, especially as this had happened before a deal on tuition fees.
The two sides are now taking part in a plenary session with all relevant commissioners, ministers and other officials.
We are expecting to hear from Britain’s PM Burnham and EU’s von der Leyen and Costa about the details of their discussions later today.
Britain ⁠and the European Union have agreed ⁠a ⁠reset deal ​and concluded negotiations on Friday, ⁠prime minister Andy Burnham’s office ⁠said.
Just to highlight Jennifer’s point there ( 10:40 ): the “hold-up” over tuition fees is nowhere near as catastrophic or dramatic as some headlines elsewhere would have you think – and, in fact, was pretty anticipated.
The three sectoral deals are still getting signed today and it counts as a genuine step forward in the post-Brexit relationship; it’s just that their full implementation get suspended until the tuition fee issue is resolved.
The explicit link on their implementation does create a new high-pressure political deadline in six months’ time, adding urgency for the two sides to resolve the tuition fees issue and unblock the whole process.
Ah, classic EU-UK negotiations stuff. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.
The arrival of Burnham and his European hosts was heavily choreographed – there were no words to the assembled media, or any shouted questions – but one notable element was the sheer number of ministers the UK PM has brought with him, in a sign of how seriously the summit is being treated by London.
These included Lou Haigh , the first secretary of state; John Healey , the chancellor; Ed Miliband , the foreign secretary; Jonathan Reynolds , the business secretary; Angela Eagle , the environment secretary, and Anneliese Midgley , the chief whip.
The two sides are now formally introducing their delegations – more handshakes!
…aaaand here they come, with an awkward three-way handshake, initiated by EU’s Costa.
Next we hear the UK’s national anthem, God Save the King, followed by the EU’s Ode to Joy. You can tell they practised ( 9:15 ).
Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset deals will not materialise unless the UK reaches a settlement with the EU over tuition fee rates for European students.
EU sources said on Friday that the three deals – on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility – will not enter into force without equal treatment for European students at British universities.
In a statement seen by the Guardian from the EU council and European Commission spelt it out:
“The Council and Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students. The Council and Commission acknowledge that these four agreements form a package of the 2026 EU-UK summit.”
The EU wants to ensure its students pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees, rather than the far higher international rate. In a concession last night, the bloc agreed to defer agreement on tuition fees by six months, but that does not mean they have accepted the UK’s position that their students pay higher rates
As the Guardian has reported, it intends to use its leverage, by making the three deals contingent on an acceptable agreement on tuition fees.
“I think our position has been clear. We think this is an issue that needs to be addressed.”
The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and the European Council president António Costa are now in position and waiting for UK’s Andy Burnham.

The European Union has struck agreements on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.
“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.
Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Burnham said that the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.
The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.
The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist radical right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.
The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister,” he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.
